style: Say in a knowledgeable, friendly way, like a museum curator
lines: Tap a pin to open a stop. Then press Play cycle and watch the circle.
Tap a ruler mark to hear a note. The piano keys underneath are only for comparison.
Each stop has a Try this switch. Flip it and listen for the change.
The badges on the pins changed. Count notes or pulses, then tap a pin to hear them.
Pick two stops in the pickers. Then press Play both cycles and listen for when they line up.
Press Play phrase, look at the ruler and the circle, then tap the pin where you think it comes from.
That's it. Tap Next mystery when you are ready.
Not there. Look at the ruler: does it use piano keys? Tap another pin.
Look at the circle. How many pulses go around? Tap another pin.
Here it is. Tap Next mystery when you are ready.
A gamelan is a set of bronze keys, gongs and drums made and tuned together.
The ud is a short-necked lute with no frets.
The sitar has movable frets and extra strings that ring by themselves.
The koto has 13 strings, each over its own movable bridge.
The bell plays one 12-pulse pattern, and every drummer keeps their place by it.
The keys are plucked with both thumbs and the right forefinger.
A siku is split into two rows of pipes, ira and arka.
Claves are two hardwood sticks struck together.
The piper blows into a bag that keeps the sound going without a break.
The erhu has two strings, and the bow hair runs between them.
